title: How to read Kenyan presidential opinion polls
summary: Five checks to make before comparing candidate percentages from different polls.

sections.heading: Start with the fieldwork dates
sections.text: A publication date tells you when findings were released. Fieldwork dates tell you when people answered. Compare those dates before interpreting a difference between two polls as a change in support.

sections.heading: Read the question and the answer choices
sections.text: A question about who someone wants to win can differ from a question about who they would vote for. Candidate lists, undecided options and the population surveyed also affect how results should be interpreted.

sections.heading: Check recruitment and methodology
sections.text: Look for the sample size, coverage, interview mode, weighting and who funded the research. A large voluntary online sample does not automatically represent the country. A reported margin of error does not resolve every potential source of bias.

sections.heading: Keep website responses separate
sections.text: Our community survey describes people who chose to respond here. It is not a nationally representative poll. Its percentages are displayed separately from published polls, and older answers without a presidential preference are excluded from that question’s denominator.

sections.heading: Return to the original publication
sections.text: Read the source and its limitations before sharing a chart. This site provides dated source links in the poll register; a source marked unverified should not be treated as a confirmed current finding.

links.label: Compare published polls and their sources

title: How to check claims about development projects
summary: Follow a project from announcement to funding, delivery and documented outcomes.

sections.heading: Identify the exact project
sections.text: Record its name, location, responsible agency and the date of the claim. Similar names and photographs from nearby sites can make unrelated projects appear connected.

sections.heading: Separate announcements from delivery
sections.text: A launch or funding announcement establishes a claim or intention. Seek dated records for procurement, spending, construction progress, completion and use before describing the project as delivered.

sections.heading: Check what photographs establish
sections.text: A photograph can provide visual context for a place at a particular time. It does not establish the full cost, funding source, occupancy, completion or impact of a project. Read the caption and date, and avoid presenting unmatched images as before-and-after evidence.

sections.heading: Keep a record of changes
sections.text: Link to the evidence, explain uncertainty and record when information changes. Our development tracker distinguishes reported commitments from the evidence still needed to assess delivery.
